tool.name: BottleneckAnalysis
tool.summary: Finds the route through a corridor polygon between two wildland blocks that maximizes the minimum corridor width encountered -- the route with the widest bottleneck, chosen over every strand and branch of the corridor at once -- and measures the corridor width at regular stations along it. Computed exactly in vector on the corridor's medial axis (a Voronoi construction); no Spatial Analyst, no raster approximation; widths and lengths are meters. An optional width threshold classifies the route into above/below stretches. Outputs the route polyline, optional station points, and optional threshold segments, each carrying the analysis record. This tool is the scripting and batch surface of the interactive Bottleneck Analysis window. A modernized port of the CorridorDesigner Evaluation Tools' Bottleneck Analysis.
tool.usage:
What this tool does. A narrow spot in a corridor is a bottleneck, and for species sensitive to edges or development a severe bottleneck can make a corridor useless. This tool finds the route between two wildland blocks that an animal preferring the widest available passage would take -- the route that maximizes the minimum corridor width encountered -- and reports the corridor width at regular stations along it, so you can see exactly where the corridor narrows, by how much, and for how long. Compare the narrowest point against what your species will tolerate; if some pinch is not constrained by hard edges (open water, development), that is where widening the corridor buys the most.
The route is provably the widest available. The corridor's medial axis (its skeleton -- every point of the axis is the center of a circle touching the boundary on two or more sides) is computed exactly from a Voronoi diagram of the corridor boundary, with the local corridor half-width known at every axis vertex. The route between the blocks is then chosen to maximize the minimum width along the way, considered over every strand, branch, and loop of the corridor simultaneously -- if two strands connect the blocks, the analysis takes the one whose narrowest point is wider, which is precisely the multi-strand question the original tool approximated with candidate routes. Among all routes achieving that widest bottleneck, the reported route is the shortest one that stays central in the widest water. (The original rasterized the corridor at 1/1000 of its extent, approximated the centerline with a streamflow-accumulation trick, and picked the best of a bundle of candidate cost paths; this version computes the same idea exactly, in vector, and typically in seconds.)
Width, measured honestly. At ~1000 stations along the route (adjustable), the corridor width is twice the exact distance from the route to the corridor boundary. The width surface is the corridor together with the two wildland block shells, matching the original: at the corridor mouths, where the corridor opens into a block, widths blend smoothly into the block landmass. The route runs from block gate to block gate, and narrowness inside a block itself never counts as a corridor bottleneck. On geographic (latitude/longitude) corridors the analysis runs in a corridor-centered azimuthal equidistant projection; widths, lengths, and thresholds are always meters, so the original's warning about hard-to-interpret geographic units no longer applies.
The threshold and the segments output. Give a width threshold in meters and the run messages report what fraction of the route is narrower, the total length below, and each below-threshold stretch's length, longest first. The optional segments output writes those stretches as an Above/Below-classified polyline feature class with the crossing points interpolated exactly. The optional station points output carries every station's distance along the route, its width, and a Below flag. The interactive window (Bottleneck Analysis in the Evaluate Corridors ribbon menu) is usually the nicer way to explore thresholds: it graphs the width profile and lets you drag the threshold live, with below-threshold stretches shown red on both the graph and the map.
Batch analyses. The original toolbar offered a separate Batch Bottleneck command driven by an 11-field parameter table. This tool replaces it: iterate the tool in ModelBuilder (or a Python loop) over your corridor/block combinations. Each output carries full metadata recording the parameters that produced it.
Corridor geometry is repaired automatically. Corridor polygons traced from rasters routinely touch themselves at cell corners (technically invalid geometry); the tool repairs this with a hair-thin buffer that also keeps such corner touches traversable -- and if the widest available route must pass through one, the tool reports an essentially zero-width bottleneck with a warning, which is the honest answer: the blocks connect only through a geometric point.
Every output knows its place in the chain. Outputs are stamped with a machine-readable record (the same Supplemental Information mechanism the other corridor tools use) naming the corridor, the blocks, every parameter, and the full width statistics, readable later by the Corridor Analysis Data Report.
Credits and references. The original CorridorDesigner Evaluation Tools are by Jeff Jenness (Jenness Enterprises), with the CorridorDesigner project by Dan Majka, Paul Beier, and Jeff Jenness; this ArcGIS Pro version is by Jeff Jenness. Please cite: Majka, D., J. Jenness, and P. Beier. 2007. CorridorDesigner: ArcGIS tools for designing and evaluating corridors. http://corridordesign.org.

dialogReference.para: The corridor to analyze -- typically a Least-Cost Corridor polygon. All features (or the layer's current selection) are treated together as the one corridor; multiple disconnected strands are handled, and blocks in different strands are reported as not connected.

param.name: corridor_expression
param.displayname: Corridor selection expression (when the layer holds several corridors)

dialogReference.para: Restricts the corridor layer to the features forming the corridor of interest -- useful when one feature class holds several corridors, or several percentile levels of one corridor. Leave blank to use every feature (or the layer's current selection).

The first wildland block: any polygon layer or feature class. Interior holes are ignored and parts not touching the corridor are dropped. May be the same layer as Wildland Block B, narrowed with the selection expression.

param.name: block_a_expression
param.displayname: Block A selection expression (when the layer holds several blocks)

dialogReference.para: Restricts the Block A layer to the features forming Block A -- for example Block = 2 on an Identify Termini output, or a name match on a wildland-blocks layer. When one layer holds exactly two recognizable blocks (a Block or Category field with two values), both expressions fill in automatically.
The second wildland block, with the same rules as Wildland Block A.

param.name: block_b_expression
param.displayname: Block B selection expression (when the layer holds several blocks)

dialogReference.para: Restricts the Block B layer to the features forming Block B.

param.name: threshold
param.displayname: Width threshold, meters (optional; classifies the route into above/below stretches)

dialogReference.para: Corridor sections narrower than this are reported (fraction of the route, total length, and each stretch's length in decreasing order) and drive the optional segments output. Leave blank to skip threshold classification -- the interactive window can explore thresholds afterward without re-running.

The widest route as a single polyline in the corridor's coordinate system, with its geodesic length, minimum (bottleneck) width, and mean width. Carries the full analysis record. A path in a folder is written as a shapefile.

One point per width station along the route: Station_m (geodesic distance along the route), Width_m, and Below (1 = narrower than the threshold; -1 when no threshold was given). The modern form of the original's ~1000-point export.
The route split into Above/Below-threshold stretches (Class and Length_m fields), with the crossing points interpolated exactly. Requires a width threshold.

param.name: n_stations
param.displayname: Number of width stations along the route

dialogReference.para: How many evenly spaced stations to measure the width at (default 1000, matching the original's point export). More stations resolve shorter pinches.

The spacing of the boundary samples that build the medial axis. Blank picks 1/2000 of the corridor extent diagonal, plenty for corridor-scale accuracy; smaller values sharpen narrow-throat widths at some speed cost.

param.name: simplify_tolerance
param.displayname: Boundary simplification tolerance, meters (blank = automatic; 0 = none)

dialogReference.para: Raster-traced corridor boundaries carry staircase noise; by default the boundary is simplified by 0.05% of the corridor's extent diagonal before analysis, which strips the staircase without moving the boundary at ecological scales. Enter 0 to analyze the boundary exactly as supplied.

param.name: profile_json
param.displayname: Profile JSON path (used by the Bottleneck Analysis window; leave blank)

dialogReference.para: Internal: where the interactive window asks this tool to write the width profile it graphs. Leave blank in normal use.

scriptExample.title: Bottleneck Analysis example (stand-alone script)
scriptExample.para: Analyzes a corridor between Blocks 2 and 3 of an Identify Termini layer with a 400 m threshold, writing all three outputs.
scriptExample.code:
import arcpy arcpy.ImportToolbox(r"C:\path\to\JennessEnterprisesTools.pyt") # your installed path is shown in this tool's run messages
arcpy.jenness.BottleneckAnalysis( r"C:\project\corridors.gdb\Corridor_Badger", "", # corridor + expression r"C:\project\corridors.gdb\Termini", "Block = 2", r"C:\project\corridors.gdb\Termini", "Block = 3", 400.0, # width threshold (m) r"C:\project\corridors.gdb\Badger_BtlRoute", r"C:\project\corridors.gdb\Badger_BtlPoints", r"C:\project\corridors.gdb\Badger_BtlSegments")
